items.item: State's primary purpose is storing bindings between remote objects and the resource instances declared in configuration, which Terraform uses to determine what changes to make

at.step: State: the tool's own record, not the live cloud

items.item: Terraform locks state automatically on any operation that could write it, silently unless acquiring the lock takes longer than expected

at.step: Locking: the guard that stops two applies colliding

items.item: Plan alone does not carry out the proposed changes; without -out=FILE it creates a speculative plan with no intent to apply it

at.step: Plan, then apply: dry run, then commit

items.item: Import requires a hand-written resource configuration block first and only imports into state, generating no configuration

items.item: HashiCorp switched Terraform's license from the MPL to the Business Source License on August 10, 2023, with little advance notice; OpenTofu is the resulting fork, created after no response by August 25, maintained under the Linux Foundation

items.item: The hook's point is that the second apply's plan was computed against an already-stale state, not that applies are inherently unsafe; a learner should be able to name exactly what made the second apply stale (an unlocked, concurrent write), not just that something went wrong

at.step: Eight seconds apart, and no error from either one

items.item: The predict step's correct answer is structural (the tool's own last-known record), not a product-specific detail; a learner should be able to state why that record can go stale before learning the vendor's chosen backend

at.step: Before the mechanism: what is a plan actually diffed against?

items.item: The locking reproduction tests a hard block on a second acquire call, not a race that sometimes loses — a learner who thinks locking just makes collisions 'less likely' has missed that a real lock either grants or refuses, with nothing in between

at.step: Locking: the guard that stops two applies colliding

items.item: Drift and import are deliberately shown as the same gap approached from two directions, not two unrelated features; a learner should be able to say which one is passive discovery and which one is the deliberate fix

items.item: The module-boundary step's point is that bundling is a review-unit decision, not a technical constraint; a learner who thinks Terraform forces three resources into one module has missed that this is a design choice this topic recommends, not a tool limitation

at.step: One unit: a bucket, its catalog entry, its IAM role

items.item: The BSL/OpenTofu step states a legal change, not a technical one — a learner who thinks Terraform 'stopped working' on the relicensing date has missed the actual claim; the real dates and license names come from OpenTofu's own account of its own founding

at.step: The license changed, and a fork answered

items.item: The Pulumi/CDK step's trade-off is specific (expressive power makes it easier to write imperative logic that breaks plan/apply safety), not a generic 'more flexible but riskier' hand-wave

at.step: A real programming language instead of a declarative file

items.item: The policy-gate reproduction's point is the enforced block itself, not a claim about how Sentinel or OPA's actual rule languages work internally; an expert reviewer should expect a minimal allow/block simulation, not a reproduction of either tool's real rule engine

items.item: The final predict step's correct answer names the policy gate specifically because it's the only listed mechanism that inspects a plan's own content before it ships; a learner who picks locking has conflated 'stops two operators colliding' with 'stops one bad plan from shipping'
